tone_statements.citation: Conrad, Agnes. 2025. A Descriptive Grammar of Eastern Minyag: An Undescribed Tibeto-Burman Language. PhD dissertation, University of Sydney (Discipline of Linguistics; supervisor Mark Post). xxi+458 pp. hdl:2123/34113.
tone_statements.quote: Eastern Minyag does not have consistent lexical tone, but a few lexical items consistently carry a high pitch. Words with a high pitch are characterized by a high F0. It is unclear whether there are any minimal pairs distinguished by pitch alone, as most lexemes do not appear to be underlyingly specified for pitch. [...] For multisyllabic lexemes, only a few disyllabic words seem to have a stable HH pitch pattern. Most appear to be otherwise unspecified for pitch, save a distinctive HL pattern reserved specifically for vocative kinship terms (§3.3.3). [...] [§2.6:] In terms of tone, Chinese dialects are all tonal, while Eastern Minyag does not have a system of lexical tone.

tone_statements.quote: またムニャ語の音調は，音節に固定したピッチを有する声調ではなく，高低のピッチパタンが緩やかに単語に被さっている音節高さアクセントである。 [注3, p.148:] …西部ムニャ語においては 2 音節語の内部に有標のアクセント核のない＊低低の組合せは存在しない。いっぽう東部ムニャ語ではごく少数ながら低低の固定ピッチを有する 2 音節語が存在する。また単音節語や語末において時に 35 のような上昇ピッチや 53 のような下降ピッチが現れることがあるが，上昇下降のピッチ移行に有意の弁別性があるわけではなく，…アクセントの識別における有標性は「音節の始まりのピッチが高い」ことにある。
tone_statements.translation: Moreover, the prosody of Mu-nya is not tone with a pitch fixed to the syllable, but a syllable-pitch accent in which a high/low pitch pattern is loosely laid over the word. [n.3, p.148:] ...in Western Mu-nya no *Low-Low combination without a marked accent nucleus exists inside a disyllabic word. In Eastern Mu-nya, on the other hand, there exist a very small number of disyllabic words with a fixed Low-Low pitch. Also, on monosyllables and word-finally a rising pitch such as 35 or a falling pitch such as 53 sometimes appears, but the rising/falling pitch movement has no significant distinctiveness, ... the marked value in identifying the accent is 'the beginning of the syllable is high in pitch'.

sources.citation: Punzi, Valentina. 2025. Fresh Twigs, Drying Blood, and Popped Corn: The Ephemeral Materiality of Eastern Minyag Ritual Objects. Religions 16(5): 539. doi:10.3390/rel16050539.
sources.note: Ethnography, no linguistics. p.3: Eastern Minyag = Qiangic-speaking community of about seven thousand people east of Gangkar (Gongga) Mountain in Shimian County; language 'not mutually intelligible with the one spoken by the Western Minyag community'; n.2 refers to Punzi 2021 for linguistic differences.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2020. Change Request 2020-043 (submitted by Agnes Conrad & Wang Baobao, 31 Aug 2020): split of mvm Muya/Minyag into Eastern Minyag [emq] and Western Minyag [wmg]; adopted 15 Jan 2021. 6 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. Identity/bibliography only: Eastern and Western Minyag mutually unintelligible ('enough divergence in the lexicon and phonology'); 'there is exceedingly little published research on Eastern Minyag'; requesters know only three published works treating it: Sun Hongkai 2016 (a word list), Yin Weibin 2012/2013 and 2017 (spatial relations).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2020. Request for New Language Code Element in ISO 639-3: Eastern Minyag [emq] (Conrad & Wang, associated with CR 2020-043). 4 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Gives names (Eastern Minyag; autonym Munya; Shimian Minyag/Munya/Muya), location (Shimian County, Jiulong County), ~2,000 speakers, oral corpus pending at ELAR; no linguistic description.

sources.citation: Bai, Junwei. 2019. A grammar of Munya. PhD thesis, James Cook University. xxx+546 pp. doi:10.25903/2SHV-X307.
sources.note: Describes WESTERN Muya (west2417; Jiangde village, Pengbuxi, northern sub-dialect): word prosody sec. 2.4 = binary /H/ vs /L/ word-tone (pitch accent-like) system; the word 'stress' never occurs. On the eastern dialect (this languoid) it has no data: sec. 1.1 'The situation in the eastern dialect area is more obscure, as there is virtually no report on the linguistic situation'; sec. 1.8 'I cannot provide any first-hand information on the eastern Munya area because I did not do any fieldwork there'; sec. 1.9 'Yin (2013, 2017).. are still the only two studies pertaining to the eastern dialect'…

sources.citation: Ikeda, Takumi. 2002. On pitch accent in the Mu-nya language. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25.2: 27-45.
sources.note: pitch accent analysis (marked /H/ vs unmarked, no spreading) of the WESTERN dialect (Sade/Shade district, Kangding). Explicitly excludes this languoid, p.27: 'All these descriptions are of the western dialect of Mu-nya, spoken around the Sade district. We have no linguistic information on the eastern dialect spoken in the Shimian district, which might be in danger of extinction.' an earlier compilation named this paper (as LTBA 25.1) for east2351; it does not describe Eastern Muya.
